title: Phở and friends
intro: Eleven things to eat and drink in Hà Nội, and the word to praise them. Most of these dishes are younger than you would think.

words.hook: Picture a friend tasting phở for the first time with a doubtful "fuh...", voice dropping, then finishing the whole bowl.
words.tip: ph sounds like f. The hỏi tone starts at your normal pitch and drops further and faster than huyền.
words.fact: Nam Định, southeast of Hà Nội (now part of Ninh Bình province), is often named as the birthplace of phở. Its modern form probably took shape between 1900 and 1907.

words.hook: Grandma calls "Come!" because the rice is ready.
words.tip: ơ is like the vowel in British "fur", with no r. Keep the tone level.

contrast.en: green rice flakes (a Hà Nội treat)

words.fact: "Ăn cơm chưa?" (have you eaten yet?) is what family and neighbours ask each other around mealtimes. Rice stands for the whole meal.

words.hook: A bundle of thin white noodles drops from the sky like a boon, and you shout "boon!" with your voice rising.
words.tip: u is the "oo" in "moon". The sắc tone rises.
words.fact: Bún chả, grilled pork with bún, is a Hà Nội dish. In 2016 Barack Obama ate it there with Anthony Bourdain.

words.hook: The crust is so crunchy it goes "bang!", and everyone at the table shouts "me!".
words.tip: In Hà Nội, anh sounds close to "ain" with a soft ng at the end. mì is "mee", falling low.
words.fact: On its own, bánh mì just means bread. The French brought the baguette in the 1860s; the famous filled sandwich took shape in Saigon in the 1950s.

words.hook: A hen settles onto her nest with a long, low "gaaa", her voice sinking like the huyền tone.
words.tip: g is soft: the back of your tongue nearly touches where English k is made, but air keeps flowing, like the g in Spanish "lago". The huyền tone starts a little below your normal pitch and falls gently, slightly breathy.
words.note: g for game bird: gà is chicken. Do not mix it up with cá (fish).
words.fact: Gà Đông Tảo, the "dragon chicken" from a village near Hà Nội, has feet so huge that hens break their own eggs, so the eggs go into incubators.

words.hook: A beefy bull gives a long, low "baw", the aw of British "saw", sinking gently like the huyền tone.
words.tip: o is open, like the "aw" in British "saw". The huyền tone falls gently.
words.note: b for beef: bò is beef, and the cow it comes from.
words.fact: Hà Nội phở is traditionally phở bò, in a clear beef broth with spring onion, coriander, pickled garlic and quẩy (fried dough). Bean sprouts and basil are a Southern habit.

words.hook: A fish leaps out of the river and you shout "ca!", your voice shooting up as you try to catch it.
words.tip: c is a k with no puff of air.
words.note: c for carp: cá is fish.
words.fact: Chả cá, turmeric fish fried at the table with dill, was so popular that Hàng Sơn Street in Hà Nội was renamed Phố Chả Cá, Grilled Fish Street.

words.hook: A mountain of fresh herbs so big you say "zow!".
words.tip: In Hà Nội, r sounds like z, so rau sounds like "zow" (rhymes with "cow"), with a short, quick a.
words.fact: Rau sống, raw greens and herbs, comes with bún chả and nem, but not with Hà Nội phở. At a Northern family meal the classic green is rau muống luộc, boiled water spinach.

words.hook: You jump into a cool lake on a hot day and come up with one quick, rising gasp: "noo-uhk!"
words.tip: ươ glides from ư (say "oo" with your lips spread) to ơ. The final c is cut short, not released.
words.fact: nước means both water and country. Đất nước, literally "land and water", is the word for homeland.

words.hook: Tea is "chai" in many languages. After the first sip you sigh "chà", your voice falling.
words.tip: In Hà Nội, tr sounds like the ch in "chip", but with no puff of air.
words.note: Hà Nội also says chè for tea (nước chè, chè xanh).
words.fact: On Hà Nội pavements, trà đá (iced tea) on tiny plastic stools is where people meet, chat and watch the traffic.

words.hook: It is the French word café, said the Vietnamese way.
words.tip: ê is like the "ay" in "say", without the glide at the end.
words.fact: Coffee is thought to have arrived with French missionaries in 1857. Vietnam is now the world's second-largest coffee producer, after Brazil, and almost all of it is robusta.

words.hook: The food is so good you start singing: "sing-ngon... ngon!".
words.tip: ng is the sound at the end of "sing". Start the word with it.

contrast.en: tip, top (of a tree or flame)

words.fact: "Ngon quá!" said to the cook is the best compliment at any street stall.

grammar.title: The main word comes first
grammar.text: In Vietnamese the thing comes first and the word that describes it follows. phở bò is pho + beef: beef pho. Describing words follow the same rule: cá ngon is tasty fish. Said on its own, Cá ngon! also means "The fish is tasty!", because Vietnamese needs no word for "is" before a describing word.

combos.note: quá after a word means "so" or "really": ngon quá! Before a word it usually means "too": quá cay, too spicy. Hà Nội people also say Ngon thế!

feature.title: Younger than the Eiffel Tower
feature.dek: Hà Nội's most famous dishes feel ancient. Most of them are not, and nearly every one has a story.
feature.pull: Chicken phở appeared in 1939, possibly because beef was not sold on Mondays and Fridays.
feature.intro: Phở feels ancient. Its modern form probably took shape between 1900 and 1907, which makes it younger than the Eiffel Tower (1889). Most of the dishes in this issue have a story like that, and you will hear them as you go.

beats.text: It probably took shape in Nam Định (since 2025 part of Ninh Bình province), southeast of Hà Nội. Its roots are still argued over: French demand for beef, Chinese beef-noodle sellers, or xáo trâu, a buffalo noodle soup sold in Hà Nội at the time.
The baguette arrived with the French in the 1860s, and bánh mì simply means bread. The stuffed sandwich the world knows took shape later, in Saigon in the 1950s.
Chicken phở appeared in 1939, possibly because beef was not sold at the markets on Mondays and Fridays.
In the late 1940s, when fresh milk was scarce, Nguyễn Văn Giảng is said to have whipped egg yolk into coffee in its place: cà phê trứng, egg coffee, still served at his family's café in Hà Nội.
Hard times shaped the menu in other ways too. In the rationing years, state shops sold phở không người lái, "pilotless phở", with no meat at all, named after American drones.

challenge.title: Street challenge
challenge.text: Order phở the Hà Nội way: "Cho tôi một bát phở bò" (a bowl of beef phở, please). Don't wait for a herb plate (Hà Nội phở has none); add a little pickled garlic, and when you finish tell the cook "Ngon quá!".
